analysis.one_liner: Writes the FTC's national do-not-call telemarketing registry into federal law.
analysis.headline: The Senate referred the bill to committee, where it died without a vote, but Congress enacted the same do-not-call registry through a separate House bill that became law days later.
analysis.plain_summary: A federal court had questioned the Federal Trade Commission's authority to run the national do-not-call registry, which lets people list their phone numbers so telemarketers cannot call them. This bill would have Congress simply ratify, or legally confirm, the FTC's registry rule from March 2003, putting it on solid statutory footing. It never got a vote in the Senate, but Congress passed the same policy days later in a separate bill that the President signed.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who do not want sales calls at home: a ratified national registry would let them put their phone numbers on a list that telemarketers are barred from calling. Phone owners gain quiet evenings and fewer interruptions; the list had drawn tens of millions of sign-ups almost immediately.

how_it_helps.text: The bill ratifies the do-not-call registry provision of the FTC's Telemarketing Sales Rule, effective March 31, 2003, confirming the rule's legal footing by statute [S2] [S3].

Congress's own finding in the bill states the FTC was authorized under the Telemarketing and Consumer Fraud and Abuse Prevention Act to compile and implement a national registry, addressing the legal question raised about the agency's power [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Telemarketing companies, which would lose the ability to call every number on the registry, cutting off a main channel for reaching potential customers. Consumers pay nothing directly; the FTC's operating costs continue as before.

drawbacks.text: The bill ratifies only the registry provision as written, which leaves the rule's existing exemptions intact; by general operation of the rule, political campaigns, charities, surveys, and companies a customer has done business with could still call numbers on the list, so many unwanted calls would remain legal [S3].

Ratifying the rule retroactively by statute sidesteps the ordinary court process for testing whether the agency stayed within its authority; a good-faith objection is that Congress was endorsing the FTC's judgment wholesale rather than weighing the policy itself [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to ordinary people is real but modest: fewer sales calls at home, at essentially no cost to anyone except telemarketers. The main weakness is that the registry, as ratified, leaves big loopholes for political, charitable, and existing-customer calls, so it quiets a nuisance rather than eliminating it. The bill was a narrow legal fix for an already popular policy, not a new program.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent the bill to the Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and the Congress ended without a vote — but by then Congress had enacted the same do-not-call registry through a separate House bill that became law, so the registry took effect anyway.

narrative.text: Senator Dianne Feinstein introduced the bill on September 24, 2003, joined by ten cosponsors, two Republicans and eight Democrats [S1] [S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day; no further action was ever recorded [S5].
The bill's entire substance was to ratify the do-not-call registry provision the FTC had already put into effect on March 31, 2003 [S2] [S3].
Because Congress enacted the do-not-call registry into law days later through a separate House bill, the death of this bill did not leave consumers without the registry.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers ended up with the do-not-call registry regardless, because Congress passed the same policy days later in a separate bill that became law. Telemarketers gained only a brief window from the court ruling questioning the FTC's authority before Congress closed it.

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ratify the FTC's do-not-call registry rule and referred it to the Commerce Committee.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's eleven sponsors were bipartisan: Senator Feinstein, a Democrat, was joined by ten cosponsors, eight Democrats and two Republicans, and there is no record of opposition to the idea itself in the action history [S4].

industries.note: A ratified national registry bars telemarketers from calling every listed household number, cutting off their main way of reaching potential customers. The industry's legal challenge to the FTC's authority is what prompted the ratification bill in the first place [S2] [S3].
